deep.reconstruction:
Context: Göttingen observatory, first days of observing with the new Repsold meridian circle, April 1818. The previous page has a clock rate and a transit-reduction formula. This page is a raw observing log for 24 April plus one reduction.

(1) Morning observations (circle in its first position).
Each row gives transit times over three wires in sidereal clock time, then a circle reading (≈ zenith distance plus an index of about 0°9'), then barometer (Paris inches z, lines l) and thermometer (°R).

Sun:
- First wire, preceding limb: 2h4m24.5s.
- Middle wire, preceding limb: 2h4m41.3s.
- First wire, following limb: 2h6m35.2s.
- Difference 2m10.7s = 130.7 s. This equals the Sun's diameter (about 31'50" = 127.3 s of time) times sec δ (δ ≈ +12.9°, sec ≈ 1.026). So the second entry is the other limb on the same wire.
- Circle readings 38°39'25" and 39°11'20.7" differ by 31'55.7", which is again the solar diameter. So both limbs were read.
- Zenith distance ≈ φ − δ ≈ 51°32' − 12°53' ≈ 38°39'.

Capella:
- Wires 5h2m59.2s, 5h3m22.5s, 5h3m45.5s.
- Arithmetic mean = 5h3m22.40s. This is exactly the value used below.
- Circle reading 5°52'34.1". Subtracting the level/zenith-point reading 0°9'31.7" (21 April) gives 5°43'02", close to φ − δ ≈ 51°31.8' − 45°48.5'.

Rigel:
- Wires 5h5m40.5s and 5h5m57.0s; the third wire is missing.
- Reduced to the mean wire this gives 5h5m56.98s. Taking the first-wire interval as about 16.25 s × sec δ (my reconstruction) gives about 56.9s.
- Circle reading 60°4'29.1".

(2) Remark, translated: in the afternoon the circle was reversed. The collimation was corrected as well as could be done on a tree trunk. To use this tree, an azimuth change was also made, in the needed sense but perhaps not of the right size. (The next page uses the 'tip of the tree in the meridian' as a mark.)

Level ('Libelle') reading, i.e. the zenith-point index of the circle:
- Provisional 0°9'19", then 0°9'20.4".
- The other microscopes read L 4'11.5" and 3'22.8" (R 3'22.7").

(3) Evening observations (circle reversed).

μ Leonis:
- Wires 9h42m9.0s, 27.2s, 45.2s.
- Intervals 18.2 s and 18.0 s, about 16.3 s × sec 26.9°.
- Reading 24°49'37.9"; other microscopes 4'30.5", 3'36.8".

Regulus:
- Wires 9h58m26.6s, 43.2s, 59m0.2s; mean 43.33s.
- Reading 38°49'44.2"; minus the level reading 9'20.4" gives 38°40'24".
- Barometer 27z2.0l, thermometer +10.1°.

(4) Logarithms.
- 0.53275 n = log10 3.41, negative (n). This is the sec δ coefficient −3.41.
- 0.46240 = log10 2.90, the tan δ coefficient. Both coefficients come from the previous page.
- 1.21378 and 1.21080 are probably logarithms of the equatorial side-wire intervals: 10^1.21378 = 16.36 s and 10^1.21080 = 16.25 s. This reading is my conjecture.

(5) Reduction of Capella and Rigel to obtain the clock error.
The previous page gives the reduction of the transit time to the true meridian:
Red = −3.65 + 2.90 tan δ − 3.41 sec δ.
- Capella, δ ≈ +45.8°: Red = −3.65 + 2.982 − 4.892 = −5.56 s.
- Rigel, δ ≈ −8.4°: Red = −3.65 − 0.42 − 3.45 = −7.53 s.
The tabular right ascensions are 5h3m14.37s (Capella) and 5h5m46.84s (Rigel). The clock error is Uhr = (T + Red) − α:
- Capella: 22.40 − 5.56 − 14.37 = +2.47 s.
- Rigel: 56.98 − 7.53 − 46.84 = +2.61 s.
The clock is therefore about 2.5 s fast, consistent with the rate of +1.00 s/day found on the previous page.
errors: No arithmetic errors found. Capella's wire mean, both reductions and both clock errors check out.
The Rigel mean-wire value 56.98 from only two wires depends on an assumed wire interval. With 16.25 s × sec δ it reproduces about 56.9–57.0, so the agreement is good but not exact to 0.01 s.

The author himself notes that the azimuth correction made in the afternoon may not have the right magnitude, so post-reversal transits (μ Leo, Regulus) carry an uncertain azimuth error. The page does not reduce them.

results.what: Reduction of meridian transits to the true meridian via Red = m + n tan δ + c sec δ, and the clock error from the difference with tabular right ascensions
results.modern_name: Transit-instrument error reduction (Bessel's/Mayer's formula: azimuth, level, collimation terms)
results.usually_credited_to: Tobias Mayer (18th c.); Bessel's standard form (c. 1820)

results.what: Mean-of-wires transit time with reduction of missing wires via equatorial wire interval × sec δ
Zenith-point determination with the level and reversal (Umlegen) of the circle; collimation adjusted on a terrestrial mark (tree)
results.modern_name: Index/zenith-point and collimation determination of a meridian circle

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine observing log from Gauss's first days with the Repsold meridian circle (1818): transits, circle readings, meteorological data and a standard clock-error reduction. Gauss's work with this instrument is well documented.

checkable.asserts: Capella wire mean (59.2 + 82.5 + 105.5)/3 = 82.40 s, i.e. 5h3m22.40s; the expression equals 0
Reduction for Capella is about -5.56 s
Reduction for Rigel is about -7.53 s
Clock error from Capella is +2.47 s
Clock error from Rigel is +2.61 s
About 16.36 and 16.25 s, plausible equatorial wire intervals
Solar diameter transit time is about 130.6 s, matching 6'35.2 - 4'24.5 = 130.7 s
1915.7 arcsec = 31'55.7", the solar diameter between the two limb readings

transcription_corrections: 'Capella 2.59.2' means 5h2m59.2s (first wire), and 'Rigel 5.40.5' means 5h5m40.5s; only the changing digits are written.
'1,21378 sec. 0,53275 n / 1,21080 tg 0,46240': the right-hand numbers are log10 of the sec δ coefficient 3.41 (negative, 'n') and the tan δ coefficient 2.90.
The struck-through reading after 'vorläufig wobei' is illegible; the surviving 'R 3'22"7' is a microscope reading.
In the Sun line the dots stand for wires that were not observed; '6'35"2' is the second limb on the first wire.
